newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa gets investment rating from Duff & Phelps.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa gets investment rating from Duff & Phelps.

text.p: Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Co of the U.S. said on Wednesday it had assigned an investment grade BBB minus rating to the foreign currency obligations of the Republic of South Africa.
The organisation said in a statement that its positive initial rating for the country reflected the strong commitment of the government to establish a competitive and creditworthy economy.

"The elements of the economic strategy include a commitment to sound fiscal and monetary policies, a well diversified economy, a growing and diversifying export base and favourable external debt ratios," it said.
However, the rating was constrained by the level of fiscal deficits, low domestic savings, high unemployment, relatively low international reserves, high income inequality and high crime rates.

The government's Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy (Gear), unveiled a year ago, had laid the foundations for sustainable growth in the future by emphasising disciplined fiscal and monetary policy, restructuring of state assets and improved labour relations.

The country was increasingly diversifying its exports away from mining towards manufacturing products, with the share of manufacturing exports rising from 35.1 percent in 1991 to 45.6 percent in 1996.

"This combined with the supply side packages in terms of mobilising investment and resources to the export sector should help in improving the overall competitiveness and export performance in the future," the agency said.
A weaker rand would also help exports, it added.

South Africa's debt indicators compared favourably with other similarly rated countries with total external debt as a percentage of GDP standing at 23.8 percent in 1996 and as a percentage of exports of goods and services at 87.7 percent.
On privatisation, Duff & Phelps said the process had yet to gain mometum but there were large potential revenues to be earned from the sale of state assets which could be used to cut the deficit.
